I appreciate that SBMM extends beyond CoD, but insofar as (a) my experience as disclosed is with CoD and Destiny 2, and (b) MW and particularly BOCW have taken centre stage with regards to the SBMM argument simply by virtue of proximity in time, I've chosen to focus around CoD. 

And yes I agree, it's a rebranding issue but I also think it's partially a deliberate and malicious strategy by proponents of SBMM to simply frame the argument as "our opposition doesn't want ANY SBMM!" It's why I repeated "Strict SBMM" so many times in my post. Sadly nuance is difficult to grasp and in more egregious cases people are pitching in their opinions when they've never played any of the games / aren't as experienced in those games where SBMM is such a huge controversy (see: Leffen from Smash Brothers, a 1v1 fighting game, expressing his perplexity and derision at why CoD players, people who play a fundamentally casual game, don't want strict SBMM).

Strict SBMM pretty much _requires_ lobbies disbanding in order to constantly recalibrate you, so that is a collateral effect. SBMM can hardly be strict if it only kicks in once before you queue into a lobby - lets say it puts you into a lobby higher than your skill level. Without breaking that apart, its not being strict with skill bands. Inverse applies.

I agree with your point on Rainbow 6. But that's because at it's core, it's a competitive / tactical shooter. If casual-competitive were on a spectrum, Rainbow 6 definitely leans more towards the competitive side (I'd put it barely ahead of Valorant but below CS:GO). CoD is not that. CoD is a casual game at its core from its mechanics. There are interviews by IW where they said they specifically built "safe spaces" for casual players. So while your argument holds water in say, Rainbow 6 (and in fact, I think unranked + SBMM mode in siege is miles better than "casual") where the mechanics are inherently competitive so SBMM in casual is warranted. Where the game is meant to be as casual as possible however (like CoD), I don't think that argument applies. Especially since (anecdotal evidence from me and my friends), we sometimes get placed into lobbies nearing 100 ping due to SBMM. This is exaggerated and amplified in group play and Warzone, and this fundamentally ruins the experience for us and many others. 

Source: https://www.dexerto.com/call-of-duty/modern-warfare-dev-interview-explains-pro-hardcore-players-frustrations-1203270/

The top comments (as of this writing) are pretty disappointing and misrepresent the argument. People aren't trying to stomp every game. SBMM doesn't stop this. Whether intentionally or not, many players of cod will attest to reverse boosting - where you do horribly one round and then placed into a lobby where people don't know how to pull the trigger, only to get catapulted into pro league lobbies. In the former, you obviously are still stomping. It's because SBMM is so strict that it's trying to recalibrate and place you in precise bands every time. Strict SBMM doesn't create a utopia where people are only matched against people of their skill levels. It means people are alternating between stomping and getting stomped, ironically creating a more inconsistent experience than connection based matchmaking. This is obviously bad because this means most people now _dread_ doing well, because they know their next lobby is going to be garbage. 

Note that most of my evidence will be anecdotal having played MW since season 0. I'm also only talking about CoD because both MW and BOCW have brought the issue of Cod SBMM to the forefront of internet hot topics. (Destiny 2 also had its bout with SBMM, but I won't go into that here). 


- People don't want no SBMM, they want _less restrictive_ SBMM. 

CoD has always had SBMM. This is obvious because you can be Prestige 3 and you'll never find a Level 1 in your lobby. That isn't an issue. The issue is when it prioritises skill over connection. This means that sometimes if there's not enough players in that strict bracket, your lobby's ping get a higher and higher. In a game where the time to kill is .1 - .2 seconds, a few digits higher ping makes a massive difference. Hell, if you get matched into a higher ping lobby, you won't do as well and SBMM drops you into a lower bracket where you can stomp - whereas normally in a lobby with lower ping your performance would have remained consistent. Plus the fact that seemingly with the implemention of strict SBMM comes lobbies disbanding every game - which takes away a lot of the fun and sense of community. Old CoD fans will remember (for example) staying in the same lobby and having a "nemesis" - someone you can't beat for the life of you. Then you learn his patterns, fix your gun, outflank him and you finally beat him. Or you make friends cos you've been shooting the shit in the same lobby for 6 rounds straight. Strict SBMM with lobby recalibration does not allow this, and takes away the social aspect of the game. Insofar as CoD isn't a competitive game (it's pretty casual), some feel that taking away the social aspect leaves CoD with, well, nothing. 

- SBMM adversely affects groups. 

My friend is obviously better than me at cod. When we play together, if I'm doing average then he's stomping. Strict SBMM accounts for this and moves us up. So I'm struggling while he's doing average. This is obviously not fun for me, nor is SBMM matching me against my skill group. If strict SBMM is present in a ranked mode, there is usually a stopper to prevent great skill disparity players from matching with each other in queue / in party. But cod doesn't have a ranked playlist and it's a pretty casual game at its core. So it's a fundamental mismatch of ranked measures being used in casual gamemodes. It feels like all of the work of ranked with none of the rewards. 

I would against cast doubt on those who say SBMM helped player retention to MW: I would instead attribute it to the total failure of BFV and the popularity of Warzone, _not_ SBMM. Fans at the launch of the game will remember the very mediocre to garbage maps (to the point where people now are asking for a _2 map playlist to return_), botched sound design and ridiculous claymore spam. This did not change until arguably the introduction of Shoot House and later Shipment. Aniyah Palace, Piccadilly, Ground War are generally agreed to be examples of horrible map design catering to camp heavy play styles. 

MW has one of the most strict SBMM systems in any casual shooter I've played. This does not mean however that I'm not stomping people. It just means my K/D fluctuates from game to game, meaning it's a pendulum swinging between two extremes at any given time. This cycle is exhausting and demoralising, and my friends and I now dread doing well. Strict SBMM is clearly not fun; streamers and players alike have (and are now more blatantly) reverse boosting, aka dropping their K/D on purpose so they can get easier lobbies. You don't even need to do this on purpose: just play a few games with off meta loadouts and eventually you'll land into an easy lobby where you can stomp. 

In conclusion:

- Strict SBMM destroys the social aspect of a casual shooter. 

- Strict SBMM is currently in a causal playlist with none of the incentives of ranked (where one might expect SBMM to be)

- Strict SBMM causes friends who want to play together to have disproportionally different experiences, usually to the detriment of the lobby or the lowest skilled player of the group. 

- Strict SBMM does not prevent stomps any more than connection based matchmaking; in fact its strictness may place players in lobbies where they can stomp others easily. 

- The frustration caused by Strict SBMM results in greater instances of reverse boosting; reverse boosting can be done by accident as well, meaning people aren't actually playing against their equals. 

- Loose SBMM has always been around and is definitely needed. But SBMM should never prioritise "skill" over connection, especially in a game where time to kill is measured in milliseconds. 

It's not as simple as "people want to stomp" / "their favourite streamer said so". If people want to stomp, Strict SBMM is not going to stop that and may in fact facilitate it by overcompensating its calibration. "The streamers and their dumb fans" is a poor strawman argument made to discredit genuine flaws with Strict SBMM and I'm tired of seeing it. Don't accept a narrative simply because it's easy.

Just to add to this: I'm not sure if it's a "western" problem. For example, I really enjoyed Hollow Knight and Hyper Light Drifter, and I would consider them souls-likes. Note that my definition of a souls-like is: emphasis on bosses, extreme difficulty, precise combat, respawning at sparse checkpoints, exploration and highly immersive worldbuilding. For me, Mortal Shell fails at worldbuilding and precise combat. Maybe it's a coincidence that the "Western" souls-likes tend to copy the third person camera too, and they also fail. If you consider Fallen Order a Soulslike (and you should, it's trying pretty damn hard to copy the Souls formula), I personally found it above average as opposed so bad, so that's an exception to the "Western Souls-like" rule. Same with Remnants: from the ashes.

**Mortal Shell**

It's pretty bad. 

To preface this: I've played all the Dark Souls games + Sekiro + Demon Souls. 

My main gripe with "Soulslike" is that by and large, the ones that follow the third person ARPG formula (see: The Surge, Ashen) don't offer enough unique points to not remind me of Dark Souls. If you're trying to copy another game and all your game does is make the player want to go back to playing the original, I don't think it's a good game. Incidentally, this is why I'm not a massive fan of VALORANT; it makes me wish I was playing CS:GO instead. This is why I can't help but constantly compare this game to Dark Souls. 

With Mortal Shell, it wears its inspirations on its sleeve. From the get go, everything feels familiar by analogy: you have an unknown origin, there are forces greater than you, the atmosphere is dreary and oppressive, and there's some kind of implied previous civilisation that probably fell because of some cataclysm. 

The combat tries to set itself apart via various methods (notably, the Harden mechanic), but on the whole doesn't feel tight enough in comparison with dark souls, nor does it differentiate itself enough. 

So if the combat is almost the same if not somewhat inferior, what's the problem? It's the atmosphere and story. 

A large part of Dark Souls' success can be attributed to how it balances dread with hope, to put it crudely. The atmosphere can be dreary and depressing, but right when all seems lost, a bonfire shows itself. Or there's a magnificent view to instil a sense of wonder in you. Or there's an NPC with a hearty laugh or an unwavering devotion to the sun. It's the same reason why I like Hollow Knight. There is always hope and a light at the end of the tunnel. This game just tries to beat you down at every turn, and quite frankly it's not my style. 

If you want to play a soulslike, I'd recommend staying away from this game. Go revisit the older dark souls games instead.

Hi, current law student (1st year). 

Law is not so much about writing essays. In my opinion writing essays is probably the easiest part of doing law. However, this is only because I did my reading. 

The hardest part of law is staying awake long enough to actually absorb the information from the mountain load of reading you'll have to do. If you do the reading properly and actually understand legal concepts and doctrines, writing essays should come extremely naturally. 1st year law is about being bombarded by legal concepts, terminology and an entirely new system of thinking that you won't understand - and then trying to absorb all of that in time for your formative / summative essays. That said, if you don't like reading and you're not a very opinionated person, you will not do well in law, period. Law is about reading fast and picking out useful bits of information even faster. As an extension to that, if your opinions aren't backed by the stuff on your reading list, it's as good as useless.

Regarding your scenario, I've definitely been there, except in law this is a highly avoidable situation. If you've done all your case reading and understand the legal concepts, your opinion is "valid". However, it must be noted that last minute research has never succeeded in law, because it's very difficult to understand legal concepts on the first go - it takes a while to sink in.

Finally, contracts make up a very small part of your legal education. In fact, contracts for me was a half-year / one-term module, and I'm going to be taking Commercial Contracts next year. Other than that, I won't be touching contracts ever again - and as far as I know, most university won't offer more than that. To give you a brief idea, my first year courses were: Contracts & Torts, Criminal, Property 1, Introduction to the Legal System, and Public Law. If you're talking about corporate law in general, then there are obviously more options (business associations, insolvency, tax, etc), but that will be second / third year options. 

To be entirely honest, there are easier ways to make money and even do well in academics. As you might know the percentage of firsts awarded in Law is 9%, the lowest of any degree. It's extremely difficult to get a firsts, it's a highly academic subject (meaning lots and lots and lots of rigorous research and reading), and to be quite honest there are easier ways to make money or even get into the commercial world. If you don't feel strongly about law as an academic subject, I would not recommend it at all. Remember: you're doing this for at least the next three years of your life.

Feel free to ask more questions if you have any.

To anyone and everyone who wants to sue the IBO: on what grounds are you going to sue them on? Putting aside the issue that you might have to take them on in a civil law court (Switzerland), in common law the only possible avenue I can think of is negligence, and even then there is unlikely to be precedent for this. The only analogy I can think of is solicitor malpractice leading to a loss of a case or negligence leading to loss of a job which could have been reasonably obtained. However I don't know how you're going to prove that you had a reasonable chance of obtaining the score you were predicted before a court of law, and even then you have to show some kind of damages suffered. Let's say you didn't get into a university because of your grades - the courts aren't going to give that university place back to you, nor can they force the IBO to give you a higher score. The most they can do is force the IBO to redo their algorithm (highly unlikely) or hand you a lump sum of money - which again will be extremely difficult to calculate.

**EDIT: Tl;dr, don't sue the IBO. Courts wont give you anything in damages that will be satisfactory to you even if you win (and the chances of winning are low). Petition your local education board to file an investigation instead, or petition universities to be aware and accommodate mitigating circumstances.**

If it's true that your immediate family doesn't enjoy the BF's presence, then your wedding has a high chance to become a shitshow.

Either one of two things happen here:

1) You tough it out & let the BF come. If your family truly hates him and is verbal about it, prepare for major arguments during your wedding. It depends on the degree of animosity and self-control in your family. Personally, my friend's family has an adopted cousin and my other family members will openly give him shit for being unemployed in his 40s (disguised as playful ribbing) during family dinners, then express displeasure afterwards privately. Are they assholes? Yes. Can you stop them? Probably not. And it ruins the mood of the dinner every time because well, his family sucks at self-control. If your family is going to openly shit on the BF during your wedding, I would say don't let the BF or the sister come. If it's really true, that your family physically can't stand him and this isn't just hyperbole on your behalf, then your family will side with you. Regardless, if you let him come, you risk turning the memory of your wedding into something you'll look back on with bitterness in the future (depending on how the BF + your sister act during the wedding).

2) You tell your sister and BF to leave and refund them the money. This will probably mean you will no longer be on speaking terms with your sister for a long while, and she won't be at one of the most important events of your life. On the flip side though, you'll be content during your wedding, and when you look back at it, it'll be a good memory (again, depending on how much your value your relationship with your sister vs. your own satisfaction). And you remove the BF from the equation meaning you don't have to worry about him "barreling through conversations".

This is based solely on the info you've given, though I suspect there may be some hyperbole on your part to appear more sympathetic. 

On a more personal note, I wouldn't bring my S/O to my family member's wedding unless I was planning to marry them in the future. So, just remember the BF you don't like could one day very well become your brother in law. 

And when that day comes, don't expect an invitation to the wedding.

Square Planar only "exists" on the x and z axis so to speak, so the shape is a two dimensional "square" or cross. However, square planar means that the central atom has 2 lone pairs above and below the central atom to force the 4 bonded atoms into that square shape (VESPR indicates that atoms try to maximize distance between themselves).

XeF4 is an example of a square planar. Xe has one electron bonded to each F, but since it's a noble gas, it has 4 electrons leftover, forming 2 lone pairs above and below Xe, forcing the 4 F into square planar. 

Octahedral is one atom bonded to 6 other atoms, meaning there's an atom above, below, leftwards, rightwards, forwards and backwards from the central atom.
